Chuck Yeager in the Bell X-1A which he flew to a record Mach 2.44 at 74,700 feet before losing control and tumbling 50,000 feet (15,240 meters) in 70 seconds before regaining control. 1953

12 December 1953: Test pilot Chuck Yeager flew the Bell X-1A rocket plane to Mach 2.44 (1,650 miles per hour/2,655 kilometers per hour) at 74,700 feet (22,769 meters), faster than anyone had flown before. After the engine was shut down, the X-1A tumbled out of control—”divergent in three axes,” in test pilot speak—and fell out of the sky. It fell 50,000 feet (15,240 meters) in 70 seconds. Yeager was exposed to accelerations of +8 to -1.5 g’s. The motion was so violent that Yeager cracked the rocketplane’s canopy with his flight helmet. He was able to recover by 30,000 feet (9,144 meters) and landed safely. He later remarked that if the X-1A had an ejection seat he would have used it. Bell engineers had warned him not to exceed Mach 2.3.

Yeager: Illegible [inaudible]—gasping—I’m down to 25,000 over Tehachapi. Don’t know whether I can get back to the base or not.
